content.text: Book reference: Chapter 13, pages 447–473. Guided Exercises: Managing Compressed Tar Archives, Transferring Files Between Systems Securely, Synchronizing Files Between Systems Securely. Lab: Archiving and Transferring Files.
RHCSA EXAM CRITICAL — This whole chapter
tar create/extract/list, scp, and rsync are all standard, hands-on RHCSA tasks — short chapter, high practical value, and genuinely useful in real sysadmin work every week.

sections.title: 13.1 tar — bundling files into one archive

content.text: A tar archive gathers many files' data plus metadata plus an index into one file, so individual members can be listed or pulled back out later. tar itself doesn't compress — compression is a separate, optional layer added on top.
| Operation (pick exactly one) | Flag |
| Create a new archive | `-c / --create` |
| Extract from an existing archive | `-x / --extract` |
| List an archive's contents (table of contents) | `-t / --list` |
| Common companion flag | Effect |
| `-f FILE` | REQUIRED alongside any operation above — names the archive file itself |
| `-v` | Verbose — show each file as it's archived/extracted |
| `-p` | Preserve exact permissions on extraction, without subtracting the umask |
WARNING — tar overwrites an existing archive with no warning
Before running tar -c with a filename, double-check nothing important already exists at that path — there's no confirmation prompt, and the old file is simply gone.
tar -cf archive.tar file1 file2 file3 # create
tar -tf archive.tar # list contents
mkdir restored && cd restored
tar -xf ../archive.tar # extract into the current directory
💡 Why this matters — Why tar strips the leading / from absolute paths

tar -cf /root/etc.tar /etc archives paths as etc/fstab, not /etc/fstab — deliberately, so that extracting the archive later can never silently overwrite unrelated files at the same absolute path on a different system. Extraction always happens relative to your current directory, which is exactly why you cd into an empty target directory first.

Reading (and therefore archiving) every file requires read permission on that file and read+execute on every containing directory — creating a full archive of /etc, for instance, genuinely requires root, since some files there aren't world-readable. An unprivileged user's tar simply skips whatever it can't read, without necessarily erroring the whole operation.
NOTE — Advanced attributes need --xattrs

Advanced attributes this course doesn't otherwise cover — ACLs and SELinux contexts — are NOT stored in a plain tar archive by default. Add --xattrs when creating the archive if you need them preserved.
Compression — three algorithms, three trade-offs
| Flag | Algorithm | Extension | Trade-off |
| `-z` | gzip | `.tar.gz (or .tgz)` | Fastest, oldest, most universally available |
| `-j` | bzip2 | `.tar.bz2` | Better compression ratio than gzip, less universally available |
| `-J` | xz | `.tar.xz` | Usually the best ratio of the three, relatively newer |
tar -czf backup.tar.gz /etc/ssh # create, gzip-compressed
tar -tf backup.tar.gz # list — no compression flag needed just to list
tar -xzf backup.tar.gz # extract — compression flag optional; tar auto-detects, but matching it is still standard practice
NOTE — Compression effectiveness depends on the data

Already-compressed formats (JPEGs, most video, RPM packages) barely shrink further under any of these three — don't expect a second round of compression to meaningfully reduce an already-compressed file.
gzip/bzip2/xz also work standalone on a single file (not just inside tar) — gzip file.tar produces file.tar.gz; reverse with gunzip/bunzip2/unxz respectively.

sections.title: 13.2 scp and sftp — secure copy over SSH

content.text: Both ride on the SSH protocol — same authentication, same encryption — so anywhere ssh already works, these do too, with no extra service to configure. Remote locations use the format [user@]host:/path — omit user@ to default to your current local username.
| Command | Direction |
| `scp localfile user@host:/remote/path` | Local → remote |
| `scp user@host:/remote/file localpath` | Remote → local |
| `scp -r user@host:/remote/dir localpath` | Recursive — copies a whole directory tree |
WARNING — Recursive scp between two servers still needs read access on the SOURCE

scp -r root@serverb:/etc/ssh ~/backup requires logging into serverb AS root (or another account that can read every file in that directory) — the destination account's own privileges are irrelevant to what can be read on the far end.
sftp — interactive file transfer
sftp user@host opens an interactive session at an sftp> prompt, starting in the connecting user's home directory on the remote end.
| sftp command | Effect |
| `ls / cd / pwd / mkdir / rmdir` | Same meaning as the local shell, but operating on the REMOTE filesystem |
| `put localfile` | Upload to the remote system |
| `get remotefile` | Download from the remote system |
| `exit` | Close the session |
RHCSA EXAM CRITICAL — scp vs. sftp — when to reach for which

scp is a single non-interactive command — ideal for scripts and one-shot copies. sftp is interactive — better when you need to browse an unfamiliar remote directory structure before deciding what to transfer. Both are fair game as the tool of choice depending on how a task is phrased.
💡 Why this matters — Why rsync exists alongside scp

scp always copies every byte, every time — fine for a one-off transfer, wasteful for repeated backups of mostly-unchanged data. rsync compares source and destination first and transfers only the differences, making every synchronization AFTER the first one dramatically faster — the same underlying advantage that makes it the standard tool for recurring backup jobs.
| Option | Effect |
| `-n / --dry-run` | Simulate only — shows what WOULD happen, changes nothing. Run this before any rsync you're not 100% sure about. |
| `-v` | Verbose progress output |
| `-a / --archive` | Shortcut bundling -r (recursive) -l (symlinks) -p (permissions) -t (timestamps) -g (group) -o (owner) -D (devices) — the standard "just preserve everything sensible" flag |
WARNING — Archive mode (-a) does NOT include hard links or extended attributes

Add -H to also preserve hard links (left out of -a by default because detecting them adds real time to the sync), -A for ACLs, and -X for SELinux contexts if your data actually depends on any of those.
rsync -av /var/log /tmp # dry run first: rsync -anv /var/log /tmp
rsync -av /var/log/ /tmp # trailing slash: syncs CONTENTS of log/, doesn't create a log/ subdirectory in the destination
rsync -av /var/log remotehost:/tmp # local → remote
rsync -av remotehost:/var/log /tmp # remote → local
RHCSA EXAM CRITICAL — The trailing-slash rule is a classic, easy-to-miss exam trap

rsync -av /var/log /tmp creates /tmp/log/ containing the directory's contents. rsync -av /var/log/ /tmp (note the trailing slash on the SOURCE) instead copies just the CONTENTS directly into /tmp, with no log/ subdirectory created at all. Bash tab-completion adds this trailing slash automatically when you tab-complete a directory name — which is exactly how this trips people up without them typing it on purpose.

Preserving ownership requires root on whichever side is the DESTINATION — remote root login (authenticate as root over SSH) if the destination is remote, or run rsync itself as root if the destination is local. Exactly one side of an rsync operation may be remote; the other must be local.

sections.title: Hands-on: practice these on your own lab

content.text: 1. On servera: tar -czf /tmp/etc-ssh-backup.tar.gz /etc/ssh — note the "Removing leading '/'" message.
2. tar -tf /tmp/etc-ssh-backup.tar.gz — confirm the contents before extracting anything.
3. mkdir /tmp/restore-test && cd /tmp/restore-test && tar -xzf /tmp/etc-ssh-backup.tar.gz — confirm the extracted structure with ls -R.
4. From workstation: scp /tmp/etc-ssh-backup.tar.gz student@serverb:/tmp/ — copy the archive across the lab.
5. sftp student@serverb, then ls, cd /tmp, get etc-ssh-backup.tar.gz, exit — pull the same file back interactively.
6. rsync -anv /etc/ssh/ student@servera:/tmp/ssh-sync/ — dry run first; drop the -n and re-run once you're confident it's doing what you expect.
7. Deliberately test the trailing-slash difference: rsync -av /etc/ssh /tmp/test1 vs. rsync -av /etc/ssh/ /tmp/test2 — compare the resulting directory structures with ls.
1. Q1 — You need to create a compressed archive of /var/www with the best possible compression ratio, and speed doesn't matter. Which tar flag do you choose?
2. Q2 — Why does rsync -av /data/ backup-server:/data/ behave differently from rsync -av /data backup-server:/data — specifically, what changes in the destination?
3. Q3 — You want to preserve file ownership when copying data with rsync from your local machine to a remote server. What does that require on the remote end?
NOTE — Answers
Q1 — -J (xz) — generally the best compression ratio of the three, at the cost of speed, which the question says doesn't matter here.

Q2 — The trailing slash on the SOURCE (/data/) syncs the CONTENTS of data/ directly into the destination path. Without it (/data), rsync creates a data/ subdirectory inside the destination and syncs into that instead — same files, one extra directory level.
Q3 — You must authenticate as root on the remote (destination) system — preserving ownership requires root privileges specifically on whichever side is the destination.
- tar -c/-x/-t (always with -f FILE) creates, extracts, or lists an archive; -z/-j/-J add gzip/bzip2/xz compression on top — tar overwrites an existing archive file with no warning.
- scp and sftp both ride on SSH, needing no separate service — scp for quick one-shot non-interactive transfers, sftp for interactive browsing of a remote filesystem.

- rsync transfers only the differences between source and destination after the first sync, making repeat backups dramatically faster than scp; -a bundles the sensible defaults (recursive, permissions, timestamps, ownership) but excludes hard links (-H) and extended attributes (-A/-X).

- A trailing slash on rsync's SOURCE directory changes whether the directory itself or just its contents get synced into the destination — a classic, easy-to-trigger-by-accident distinction via tab-completion.
